title: The Bigfoot mystery is fascinating. The family story is even better
excerpt: "Capturing Bigfoot" revisits the Patterson-Gimlin film and reveals new evidence about the famous Northern California footage.
content:
That famous footage of Bigfoot trudging around a Northern California forest nearly 60 years ago has once and for all been exposed as a hoax.

But in the endlessly fascinating "Capturing Bigfoot," that's just the headline. The story of the footage and how it came to destroy families and friendships is both wild and deeply moving.

Director Marq Evans' engrossing documentary, which premiered in March at South by Southwest in Austin, Texas, is now available to rent or purchase on Prime Video. 

What has become known as the Patterson-Gimlin Film was shot on Oct. 20, 1967, in Del Norte County, south of the Oregon border. Lasting only 59 seconds, it seems to show a female Bigfoot, dubbed "Patty," ambling into the forest.

Bigfoot, aka Sasquatch, is a large ape-like humanoid that has been part of Native American and other Indigenous North American cultures' folklore for centuries, although there is no verified sighting of such a creature.

More Information

"Capturing Bigfoot": Documentary. Directed by Marq Evans. (Not rated. 102 minutes.) Available on Prime Video to rent or purchase. Also available through www.capturingbigfoot.com. 

The film was shot by Roger Patterson, a self-described Bigfoot hunter, with assistance from Robert Gimlin. For years, the footage was parsed and examined and obsessed over much like that decade's other famous home movie, the Zapruder film that captured President John F. Kennedy's assassination.

Patterson, who died of cancer in 1972, and Gimlin always maintained the authenticity of the footage. Even experts had trouble debunking it.

Then in 1999, a man named Bob Heironimus claimed to be the man in the Bigfoot costume and passed a lie detector test on live television.

Still, many didn't buy the claim. Bigfoot conferences and conventions generally dismissed Heironimus' claims.

"Capturing Bigfoot" uncovers one major piece of evidence, but focuses on Patterson's son, Clint, and the central figures who are still alive, including Gimlin and Patterson's mother, Patricia, as well as other Bigfoot experts.

What's heartbreaking is what happened when Patterson became something of a cult hero and realized the film could lead to big money. He and a brother-in-law, Al Deatley, created a docudrama that included the footage and showed it in movie theaters, making the equivalent of $5 million today.

But he and Deatley had a falling out, and Deatley ended up with most of the loot. After Patterson's death, the rights to the film passed to his widow, and she was able to make a living licensing the footage to television shows.

Years later, when Clint Patterson wanted to investigate the possibility that his father's film was a hoax, his mother broke off contact. When "Capturing Bigfoot" opens, they hadn't spoken in eight years.

In a twist, Evans and his team discover what turns out to be rehearsal footage, kept in a safe for nearly six decades by the man who developed the film, that proves the Patterson-Gimlin film to be a hoax.

Strangely, it turns out to be a source of healing for all involved.

Although the Patterson-Gimlin footage turns out not to be authentic, "Capturing Bigfoot" is. Evans steeps his documentary in Bigfoot lore showing what an industry it has become, especially in the rural Northwest. He gives them mad respect, even as he upends their world.
